entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Athena Nike on the Athenian Acropolis, built c. 425-420 BCE in the Ionic order by the architect Callicrates — the same architect who co-designed the Parthenon — is a small but exquisitely proportioned amphiprostyle temple (4 columns on each short end) dedicated to Athena as goddess of victory (nike). It stands on the southwestern bastion of the Acropolis, commanding views over the Saronic Gulf, and its frieze depicted the Battle of Marathon and mythological battles between Greeks and Persians and Greeks and Giants.

The temple was dismantled by the Ottomans in 1686 to build a gun battery (the same year they blew up the Parthenon) and its stones were incorporated into a defensive wall. The temple was reconstructed from the scattered blocks in 1836-1842 under the newly independent Greek state — one of the first systematic archaeological reconstructions in history — and again more carefully in 1998-2010 using improved anastylosis techniques.

The Temple of Athena Nike represents the peak of Ionic refinement at the Athenian Acropolis building program (Periclean era, c. 450-400 BCE): its sculptural frieze, the balustrade around the bastion (c. 410 BCE) depicting winged Nikes adjusting their sandals, and its perfect proportions within a confined space demonstrate the Athenian achievement of architectural harmony. The balustrade Nike reliefs — particularly the 'Nike fastening her sandal' (now in the Acropolis Museum) — are among the most admired works of 5th-century BCE Greek sculpture.
